label: thm:scalar-expectation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:scalar-expectation}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group and let
$\sigma$ be a pointwise weakly mixing trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on a tracial von Neumann algebra $(Q,\tau_Q)$. If
${\mathcal P}\subseteq Q\rtimes\Gamma$ is a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann
subalgebra and $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})={\mathbb C}1$, then
${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)$. The same conclusion holds for a subalgebra
${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes Q$ invariant under the diagonal
action and satisfying $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})={\mathbb C}1$. In  both cases, if $\Gamma$ also has the
ISR property, then ${\mathcal P}=L(N)$ for some $N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$.

label: thm:cs-intro
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cs-intro}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group and let
$\sigma$ be a trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on a tracial von Neumann algebra $(Q,\tau_Q)$.
Let ${\mathcal P}\subseteq Q\rtimes\Gamma$ be a $\Gamma$-invariant von
Neumann subalgebra such that $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})\subseteq{\mathcal P}$, and let
$B=\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})$. If the action  $\sigma$ is pointwise weakly mixing relative to $B$, then ${\mathcal P}\subseteq B\rtimes\Gamma$.
The same holds for a von Neumann subalgebra of $L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes Q$
invariant under the diagonal action, where now 
$\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B$ and the conclusion is
${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes B$.

label: thm:main-tensor
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-tensor}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable group with trivial amenable radical and
the ISR property. Let
$\sigma$ be a p.m.p.~action of $\Gamma$ on $(X,\nu)$ which
is pointwise weakly
mixing relative to every proper $\Gamma$-factor, including the
trivial factor. If
${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimesL^\infty(X,\nu)$ is invariant under the
diagonal action, then ${\mathcal P}=L(N)\bar\otimes B$ and
$Z({\mathcal P})={\mathbb C}1\bar\otimes B$
for some normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$ and some
$\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra $B\subseteqL^\infty(X,\nu)$.

label: thm:intro-prime
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-prime}
For every $2\leq n\leq\infty$, there exists an essentially free, prime, pointwise
weakly mixing p.m.p.~action of ${\mathbb F}_n$. These actions may be
obtained by restricting a single action of ${\mathbb F}_2$ to an increasing
family of free subgroups.

label: cor:intro-free
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:intro-free}
Let $\sigma$ be an essentially free, prime,
pointwise weakly mixing p.m.p.~action of ${\mathbb F}_n$ on $(X,\nu)$, where
$2\leq n\leq\infty$. If ${\mathcal P}\subseteqL^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes{\mathbb F}_n$ is invariant
and ${\mathcal P}\capL^\infty(X,\nu)\neq{\mathbb C}1$, then ${\mathcal P}=L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes N$ for some
$N\trianglelefteq{\mathbb F}_n$. If $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})={\mathbb C}1$, then
${\mathcal P}=L(N)$ for some $N\trianglelefteq{\mathbb F}_n$.

label: def:central-free
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:central-free}
Consider a trace-preserving  action $\sigma$ of a countable group $\Gamma$ on a tracial von Neumann algebra $Q$.
A $\Gamma$-invariant inclusion $B\subseteq Q$ is \emph{centrally
$\Gamma$-free} if, for each $s\in \Gamma, s\ne e$, there are countably many
projections
$p_j\in B^\omega\cap Q'$ ($j \in {\mathbb N}$) such that $\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j=1$ \textup{(}in the strong
operator topology\textup{)} and
$p_j\sigma_s^\omega(p_j)=0$ for every $j\in {\mathbb N}$.
head: environment

label: lem:central-free-expectation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:central-free-expectation}
Suppose that $\sigma$ is a trace-preserving  action  of a countable group $\Gamma$ on a tracial von Neumann algebra $Q$. Let $B$ be a $\Gamma$-invariant subalgebra of $Q$ such that  $B\subseteq Q$ is centrally $\Gamma$-free. Then
$\mathbb{E}(x)\in W^*(B,x)$ for every $x\in Q\rtimes_\sigma\Gamma$,
and $B'\cap(B\rtimes_\sigma\Gamma)=Z(B)$. Here, $W^*(B, x)$ denotes the von Neumann subalgebra of $Q\rtimes_{\sigma}\Gamma$ generated by $B$ and $x$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first assertion, we follow the argument in
\cite[Theorem~4.6]{Suz}.

We shall write $M:=Q\rtimes_\sigma\Gamma$. Let $x\in M$, and consider $D=W^*(B,x)$.  We can write
$x=\sum_{t\in\Gamma}x_tu_t$, where
$x_t=\mathbb{E}(xu_t^*)\in Q$. Fix $s \in \Gamma, s\ne e$, and choose projections
$p_j\in B^\omega\cap Q'\subseteq D^\omega$ as in Definition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{def:central-free}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  .
These projections are pairwise orthogonal. 
For $y\in M^\omega$, define $\Phi(y)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_jyp_j$.
The partial sums have norm at most $\|y\|$, and
\[
\sum_j\|p_jyp_j\|_2^2\le\sum_j\|p_jy\|_2^2=\|y\|_2^2.
\]
Since the summands are orthogonal in $L^2(M^\omega)$, the partial sums
are $\|\cdot\|_2$-Cauchy. Therefore $\Phi(y)\in M^\omega$, with
$\|\Phi(y)\|\le\|y\|$ and $\|\Phi(y)\|_2\le\|y\|_2$.
Let $\Psi=\mathbb{E}_M\circ\Phi$, with $\mathbb{E}_M$ as in fact~(2) above.
Then $\Psi$ is contractive in both the operator norm and the $L^2$-norm. For $y\in D$, the partial
sums defining $\Phi(y)$ belong to $D^\omega$ and have norm at most
$\|y\|$, so their $\|\cdot\|_2$-limit also belongs to $D^\omega$.
Since $\mathbb{E}_M(D^\omega)=D$, we get $\Psi(D)\subseteq D$.

We shall now compute the Fourier coefficients of $\Psi(y)$ for $y=\sum_{t\in \Gamma}y_tu_t\in M$.
For $t\in\Gamma$, fact~(3) gives $u_tp_j=\sigma_t^\omega(p_j)u_t$, so
$\Phi(y_tu_t)=c_tu_t$, where
$c_t=\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_jy_t\sigma_t^\omega(p_j)$.
The partial sums defining $c_t$ belong to $Q^\omega$, have norm at most
$\|y_t\|$, and converge in $\|\cdot\|_2$. Thus $c_t\in Q^\omega$.
Bimodularity gives $\Psi(y_tu_t)=\mathbb{E}_M(c_t)u_t$, where
$\mathbb{E}_M(c_t)\in Q$. By linearity and $\|\cdot\|_2$-contractivity,
$\Psi(y)=\sum_{t\in \Gamma}\mathbb{E}_M(c_t)u_t$ in $L^2(M)$.
Since the projections $p_j$ are pairwise orthogonal,
\[
\|\mathbb{E}_M(c_t)\|_2^2\le\|c_t\|_2^2
=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\|p_jy_t\sigma_t^\omega(p_j)\|_2^2
\le\sum_{j=1}^\infty\|p_jy_t\|_2^2=\|y_t\|_2^2.
\]
Since $p_j$ commutes with $y_t\in Q$, we have $c_e=y_e$ and
$c_s=y_s\sum_{j=1}^\infty p_j\sigma_s^\omega(p_j)=0$.
Thus $\Psi$ maps $D$ into $D$, fixes the Fourier coefficient at $e$,
annihilates the coefficient at $s$, and does not increase the
$\|\cdot\|_2$-norm of any Fourier coefficient. 

Now let $F\Subset\Gamma\setminus\{e\}$, write $F=\{s_1,\ldots,s_k\}$, and let
$\Psi_i$ be the map constructed above for $s=s_i$. Set $x^{(0)}=x$ and
$x^{(i)}=\Psi_i(x^{(i-1)})$ for $1\le i\le k$. Then $x^{(k)}\in D$ and
$\|x^{(k)}\|\le\|x\|$. Its Fourier coefficient at $e$ is $x_e$, its
coefficients at the elements of $F$ vanish, and its coefficient at any
$t$ has $\|\cdot\|_2$-norm at most $\|x_t\|_2$. Hence
\[
\|x^{(k)}-\mathbb{E}(x)\|_2^2\le\sum_{t\notin F\cup\{e\}}\|x_t\|_2^2.
\]
Taking an increasing sequence of finite sets $F$ exhausting
$\Gamma\setminus\{e\}$, we obtain a sequence in $D$, bounded in norm by
$\|x\|$, which converges to $\mathbb{E}(x)$ in $\|\cdot\|_2$.
Since the ball of radius $\|x\|$ in $D$ is $\|\cdot\|_2$-closed in $M$,
we conclude that $\mathbb{E}(x)\in D$.

For the second assertion, let $x=\sum_{s\in \Gamma}a_su_s\in B'\cap(B\rtimes_\sigma\Gamma)$,
where $a_s\in B$. Comparing the Fourier coefficients of $bx$ and $xb$
gives $ba_s=a_s\sigma_s(b)$ for every $b\in B$ and $s\in\Gamma$.
Fix $s\ne e$ and choose the projections $p_j$ as in
Definition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{def:central-free}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  . The same identity in the ultrapower,
applied to representing sequences in $B$,
gives $p_ja_s=a_s\sigma_s^\omega(p_j)$  for every $j \in {\mathbb N}$. Since $p_j$ commutes with
$a_s$, multiplication on the right by $p_j$ gives $a_sp_j=a_s\sigma_s^\omega(p_j)p_j
=a_s(p_j\sigma_s^\omega(p_j))^*=0$.
Summing over $j$ yields $a_s=0$. Thus $x=a_e\in Z(B)$.
The reverse inclusion is immediate.

label: lem:boundary-covariance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundary-covariance}
Write $(g\cdot f)(x)=f(g^{-1}x)$ for $g\in\Gamma$, $f\in C(Z)$ and
$x\in Z$. Then
$v_sm_fv_s^*=m_{s\cdot f}$ and $u_tm_fu_t^*=m_{t\cdot f}$ for $s,t\in\Gamma$,
equivalently $u_t^*m_f=m_{t^{-1}\cdot f}u_t^*$ with $(t^{-1}\cdot f)(x)=f(tx)$. Moreover,
$C(Z)$ commutes with $\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}Q$ inside $\mathbb B(L^2(\widetilde{M}))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first relation we have
\begin{align*}
v_s m_f v_s^*(\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h)
&=v_s m_f(\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_{s^{-1}h})\\
&=f(s^{-1}hrx_0)\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h\\
&=(s\cdot f)(hrx_0)\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h
=m_{s\cdot f}(\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h),
\end{align*}
and for the second,
\begin{align*}
u_t m_f u_t^*(\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h)
&=u_t m_f(\delta_{h^{-1}t^{-1}hr}\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h)\\
&=u_t\bigl(f(t^{-1}hrx_0)\delta_{h^{-1}t^{-1}hr}\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h\bigr)\\
&=f(t^{-1}hrx_0)\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h\\
&=(t\cdot f)(hrx_0)\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h
=m_{t\cdot f}(\delta_r\otimes\eta\otimes\delta_h).
\end{align*}
The final assertion holds because both $C(Z)$ and $\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}Q$ act diagonally in the
two $\ell^2(\Gamma)$-coordinates, the former by scalars on each fibre.

label: def: relative weak mixing
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def: relative weak mixing}
Let $\alpha$ be a trace-preserving automorphism of $(Q,\tau_Q)$ and let
$B\subseteq Q$ be an $\alpha$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra.
The automorphism $\alpha$ is \emph{weakly mixing relative to $B$} if
$\frac1m\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}\lVert\mathbb{E}_B(\zeta^*\alpha^n(\xi))\rVert_2^2\to0$ as $m\to\infty$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in Q$ with
$\mathbb{E}_B(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_B(\zeta)=0$.
For $B={\mathbb C}1$, this is \emph{weak mixing}.
A trace-preserving action $\sigma$ of $\Gamma$ on $(Q,\tau_Q)$ is
\emph{pointwise weakly mixing relative to $B$} if $B$ is
$\Gamma$-invariant and $\sigma_g$ is weakly mixing relative to $B$
for every $g\ne e$. For $B={\mathbb C}1$, we say that $\sigma$ is
\emph{pointwise weakly mixing}.

label: lem:relative-pairwise-wm-selection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:relative-pairwise-wm-selection}
Let $\alpha$ be a trace-preserving automorphism of $(Q,\tau_Q)$ which
is weakly mixing relative to an $\alpha$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra
$B\subseteq Q$, and let $\Xi\Subset Q$ be finite. Then there exists a strictly increasing sequence
$(m_k)_{k\ge1}\subseteq{\mathbb N}$ such that
$\|\mathbb{E}_B(\eta^*\alpha^{m_\ell-m_k}(\xi))\|_2\to0$ as
$\max\{k,\ell\}\to\infty$ with $k\neq\ell$, for all
$\xi,\eta\in\Xi$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}_B(\xi)=\mathbb{E}_B(\eta)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Xi_0=\{\xi\in\Xi\mid\mathbb{E}_B\xi=0\}$. If $\Xi_0$ is empty, any
strictly increasing sequence works. Otherwise, for $\xi,\eta\in\Xi_0$, set
$q_{\xi,\eta}(n)=\|\mathbb{E}_B(\eta^*\alpha^n(\xi))\|_2$.
For each positive integer $r$, relative weak mixing implies that
$\{n\ge1\mid q_{\xi,\eta}(n)\ge1/r\}$ has density zero, since its proportion
in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is bounded by
$r^2N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^Nq_{\xi,\eta}(n)^2$.
Equivariance, preservation of adjoints and invariance of the $L^2$-norm give
$q_{\xi,\eta}(-n)=q_{\eta,\xi}(n)$. Hence
$S_r=\{n\ge1\mid\max_{\xi,\eta\in\Xi_0}\max_{\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}} q_{\xi,\eta}(\varepsilon n)<1/r\}$
has density one. Choose $m_1\ge1$ and, recursively, choose
$m_k>m_{k-1}$ in $\bigcap_{j<k}(m_j+S_k)$; this finite intersection has
density one. If $\ell>k$, then $m_\ell-m_k\in S_\ell$; if $k>\ell$,
use the negative-time inequality from $S_k$. The required norm is thus
less than $1/\max(k,\ell)$ for every unequal pair of indices.

label: lem:weak-zero-from-pairwise
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As closed balls in $\widehat{\mathcal H}$ are weakly sequentially compact, it suffices to show that every weak cluster point of $(\eta_k)_{k \in {\mathbb N}}$ equals $0$. Let $\eta\in\widehat{\mathcal H}$ and suppose that $\eta_{k_\ell}\to\eta$
weakly as $\ell$ tends to infinity. Fix $j\in {\mathbb N}$. Since $\langle\eta_{k_j},\eta_{k_\ell}\rangle\to0$ as $\ell\to\infty$, we see that $\langle\eta_{k_j},\eta\rangle=0$. Letting $j\to\infty$ and
using again the assumed weak convergence gives $\|\eta\|^2=0$. Thus $\eta=0$.

label: lem:stinespring-l2-small
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:stinespring-l2-small}
Let $(N,\tau)$ be a tracial von Neumann algebra, let $Q\subseteq N$ be a von Neumann subalgebra, and
let $\mathbb{E}_Q$ be the trace-preserving conditional expectation from $N$ onto $Q$. Let $(a_k)_{k\in{\mathbb N}}$ and $(b_k)_{k\in{\mathbb N}}$
be bounded sequences of elements in $N$. Assume that
$\|\mathbb{E}_Q(a_ka_\ell^*)\|_2\to0$ as $\max\{k,\ell\}\to\infty$, $k\neq\ell$. Then
$b_k\mathbb{E}_Q(a_k)\to0$ in the weak operator topology as $k$ tends to infinity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(\pi,\widehat{{\mathcal H}},V)$ be a Stinespring dilation for $\mathbb{E}_Q$, viewed as a u.c.p.\ map on
$N\subseteq \mathbb B(L^2(N, \tau))$, so that $\mathbb{E}_Q(x)=V^*\pi(x)V$ for $x\in N$ (\cite[Theorem~1.5.3]{BroOza08}). For each $k \in {\mathbb N}$ set
$T_k=b_kV^*\pi(a_k)\in \mathbb B(\widehat{{\mathcal H}};L^2(N, \tau))$. Then for $k, \ell \in {\mathbb N}$ we have
$T_kT_\ell^*=b_k\mathbb{E}_Q(a_ka_\ell^*)b_\ell^*$.
Fix $\eta\in N$. Setting $z_{k,\ell}=\mathbb{E}_Q (a_ka_\ell^*)$ we have
\[
|\langle T_k^*\eta,T_\ell^*\eta\rangle|=|\tau(\eta^*b_{\ell}z_{\ell,k}b_k^*\eta)|\le
\|b_k^*\eta\eta^*b_{\ell}\|_2\|z_{\ell,k}\|_2.
\]
Since $(b_k)_{k\in{\mathbb N}}$ is bounded, the displayed expression tends to $0$
as $\max\{k,\ell\}\to\infty$, $k\neq\ell$. By approximation and the uniform bound on
$(T_k)_{k\in {\mathbb N}}$, the same holds for every $\eta\in L^2(N,\tau)$. Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:weak-zero-from-pairwise}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   gives
$T_k^*\eta\to0$ weakly for every $\eta\in L^2(N, \tau)$. Thus also $b_k\mathbb{E}_Q(a_k)=T_kV\to0$ in the weak operator topology.

title: Definition
body_md: A group $\Gamma$ satisfies the unique roots property if for every $g\in \Gamma$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ there exists at most one $f\in \Gamma$ such that $f^n=g$.
head: environment

label: def:strongeci
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:strongeci}
A group $\Gamma$ satisfies the ECI property if for every
$e\neq g\in \Gamma$ and every pair of
finite sets $F\Subset \Gamma\setminus C_\Gamma(g)$ and $R \Subset \Gamma$ there exists $N \in {\mathbb N}$ such that
$g^{n}Fg^{-n}\cap R=\emptyset$ for all $n >N$.
head: environment

label: lemma: unique roots -> ECI
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: unique roots -> ECI}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable ICC group. Then it satisfies the ECI property if and only if it satisfies    the unique  roots property.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume that $\Gamma$ is non-trivial.

Assume that $\Gamma$  satisfies    the unique roots property.    Fix $g\in \Gamma\setminus \{e\}$ and let $f\in \Gamma\setminus C_\Gamma(g)$. Assume that there exist $n,m\in\mathbb N$, $n<m$, such that $g^nfg^{-n}=g^mfg^{-m}$. Then we have
    $(f^{-1}gf)^{m-n}=f^{-1}g^{m-n}f=g^{m-n}$. The unique roots property implies that $f^{-1}gf=g$, which contradicts the fact that $f$ does not belong to the centralizer of $g$. Thus, the elements $g^nfg^{-n}$, $n\in\mathbb N$, are pairwise distinct.

   Now let $F\Subset \Gamma\setminus C_\Gamma(g)$ and $R \Subset \Gamma$ be finite sets.
For each $f\in F$ and $r\in R$, there is at most one $n\in{\mathbb N}$ such that $g^nfg^{-n}=r$.
Thus there are only finitely many such integers. Choose $N\geq1$ larger than all of them,
taking $N=1$ if there are none. Then $g^nFg^{-n}\cap R=\emptyset$ for every $n>N$, proving ECI.

     Assume then that $\Gamma$ has the ECI property and does not have the unique  roots property. Then there exist $g\neq h\in \Gamma$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ such that $g^n=h^n$. Assume first $g,h\neq e$. If $h\notin C_\Gamma(g)$, set $F=\{g^ihg^{-i}\mid i=0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Clearly, $F\subseteq \Gamma\setminus C_\Gamma(g)$, but $gFg^{-1}=F$, which contradicts the ECI property. Let then $h\in C_\Gamma(g)$. Then $(h^{-1}g)^n=e$. Thus, we arrive at the case $g^n=e$ for some $g\neq e$. As $\Gamma$ is assumed to be ICC, $g$ cannot belong to the centre of $\Gamma$. Take $h$ not commuting with $g$ and set $F$ as above. We then again obtain a contradiction to the ECI property, which finishes the proof.

label: lem:commuting-square
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: rem:cs-crossed
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:cs-crossed}
Let $\sigma$ be a trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on a tracial von Neumann algebra $(Q,\tau_Q)$ and let
${\mathcal P}\subseteq Q\rtimes_\sigma\Gamma$ be a von Neumann subalgebra. For $A=Q$ we have
$\mathbb{E}_A=\mathbb{E}$, so ${\mathcal P}$ and $Q$ form a commuting square if and only if
$\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})\subseteq{\mathcal P}$. In this case $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})={\mathcal P}\cap Q$ and
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})}(f)$ for every $f\in Q$. If, moreover, ${\mathcal P}$ is
$\Gamma$-invariant, then $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})$ is a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra of $Q$.
When $(Q,\tau_Q)=(L^\infty(X,\nu),\nu)$, this means that $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})=L^\infty(Y,\eta)$ for a $\Gamma$-equivariant factor map
from $(X,\nu)$ to $(Y,\eta)$. In the scalar case, Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:commuting-square}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   shows that $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})={\mathbb C}1$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(f)=\tau_Q(f)1$ for every
$f\in Q$. Every
algebra of the form $B\rtimes N$ forms a commuting square with $Q$. For a p.m.p.~action, the same remarks apply to
$L(\Gamma)\bar\otimesL^\infty(X,\nu)$, with $A=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}L^\infty(X,\nu)$.

label: thm:cs-engine
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cs-engine}
Let $(M,\tau)$ be a tracial von Neumann algebra, let $\theta$ be a trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on $M$, and let $A\subseteq M$ be a $\theta$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra.
Write $\sigma=\theta|_A$. Let ${\mathcal P}\subseteq M$ be a
$\theta$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra which forms a commuting square with $A$, and let
$B={\mathcal P}\cap A$. Let $g\in\Gamma$ and let $w\in M$ be a unitary with $\theta_g(w)=w$. If $\sigma_g$
is weakly mixing relative to $B$, then $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(fw)=0$ for every
$f\in A$ with $\mathbb{E}_B(f)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since ${\mathcal P}$ is $\theta$-invariant and $\theta$ preserves $\tau$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$
is $\theta$-equivariant; also $B$ is $\sigma$-invariant, so $\mathbb{E}_B$ commutes with $\sigma_g$.
By Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:commuting-square}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  , $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(a)=\mathbb{E}_B(a)$ for every $a\in A$.

Fix $f\in A$ with $\mathbb{E}_B(f)=0$; then also $\mathbb{E}_B(f^*)=0$. Apply
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:relative-pairwise-wm-selection}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup

body_md:
\label{lem:groupoid-to-normal}
Let $\sigma$ be a trace-preserving action of a countable group $\Gamma$ on a tracial
von Neumann algebra $(B,\tau_B)$. Suppose that $B'\cap(B\rtimes\Gamma)=Z(B)$ and that
$\sigma_s$ is ergodic for every $s\neq e$. If $B\subseteq{\mathcal P}\subseteq B\rtimes\Gamma$
is a $\Gamma$-invariant intermediate von Neumann algebra, then ${\mathcal P}=B\rtimes N$ for the
normal subgroup $N=\{s\in\Gamma\mid u_s\in{\mathcal P}\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the canonical conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ is $\Gamma$-equivariant, that is,
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_gxu_g^*)=u_g\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(x)u_g^*$ for all $g\in\Gamma$ and $x\in B\rtimes\Gamma$.

Fix $e\neq s\in \Gamma$ and let $v_s=u_s^*\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)$. We claim that
$v_s\in{\mathcal P}'\cap(B\rtimes \Gamma)$. Indeed, for $m\in{\mathcal P}$ let
$\tilde{m}=u_s^*mu_s\in{\mathcal P}$. Using ${\mathcal P}$-bimodularity of $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ twice, we obtain
\[
\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)\tilde{m}=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s\tilde{m})=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(mu_s)=m\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s),
\]
whence $v_s\tilde{m}=u_s^*m\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=\tilde{m}v_s$. As $m\mapsto \tilde{m}$ is a bijection of ${\mathcal P}$, the
claim follows. Since $B\subseteq{\mathcal P}$, our assumption gives
$v_s\in{\mathcal P}'\cap(B\rtimes\Gamma)\subseteq B'\cap(B\rtimes\Gamma)=Z(B)$.

                                      
By equivariance of $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ we have
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=u_s\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)u_s^*$, that is,
$u_s^*\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)u_s^*$, and therefore $\sigma_s(v_s)=u_sv_su_s^*=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)u_s^*=v_s$.
Since $\sigma_s$ is ergodic on $B$, we get $v_s=c_s1$ for some $c_s\in{\mathbb C}$, that is,
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=c_su_s$. Applying $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ once more and using idempotence yields
$c_s^2=c_s$, so $c_s\in\{0,1\}$. Thus for every $s\in \Gamma$, either $u_s\in{\mathcal P}$ or
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=0$.

Let $N=\{s\in \Gamma\mid u_s\in{\mathcal P}\}$. Then $N$ is a subgroup, and it is normal because
$u_gu_su_g^*=u_{gsg^{-1}}$ for all $s, g \in \Gamma$ and ${\mathcal P}$ is $\Gamma$-invariant. Clearly
$B\rtimes N\subseteq{\mathcal P}$. Conversely, let $x\in{\mathcal P}$ and $s\in \Gamma \setminus  N$. For every $b\in B$,
bimodularity gives $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(bu_s)=b\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(u_s)=0$, hence
$\langle x,bu_s\rangle=\langle x,\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(bu_s)\rangle=0$.
Thus the $s$-th Fourier coefficient of $x$ vanishes. Hence $x\in B\rtimes N$, and
${\mathcal P}=B\rtimes N$.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{rem:nonicc-ideals}\upshape
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial countable group that is not ICC, and let
$\Gamma\curvearrowright(X,\nu)$ be a p.m.p.~action on a nonatomic
probability space. Then $L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma$ admits a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra that contains
$L(\Gamma)$ and is not of the form $B\rtimes\Lambda$ in the canonical embedding.

Indeed, let $p \in Z(L(\Gamma))$ be a non-trivial projection. 
                                                         
                                                          
                                                                     
                                   
Set ${\mathcal P}=p(L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma)p\oplus p^{\perp}L(\Gamma)$. Then                                     
                 
${\mathcal P}$ is a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra which contains $L(\Gamma)$.                            
                                   

We claim that ${\mathcal P}\cap L^\infty(X,\nu)={\mathbb C}1$. If $a\in{\mathcal P}\cap L^\infty(X,\nu)$, then $a$
commutes with $p^{\perp}$ and $p^{\perp}ap^{\perp}$ belongs to $p^{\perp}L(\Gamma)$. Bimodularity of the
trace-preserving expectation onto $L(\Gamma)$ gives
$p^{\perp}ap^{\perp}=\mathbb{E}_{L(\Gamma)}(p^{\perp}ap^{\perp})=\nu(a)p^{\perp}$.
Thus, $(a-\nu(a)1)p^{\perp}=0$. Applying $\mathbb{E}$ to
$(a-\nu(a)1)p^{\perp}(a-\nu(a)1)^*$ gives
$\tau(p^{\perp})|a-\nu(a)1|^2=0$, proving the claim.

On the other hand, $\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})\ne{\mathbb C}1$. Indeed, write
$p=\sum_{g\in\Gamma}p_g u_g$ and choose a measurable set $D$ with
$0<\nu(D)<\tau(p)$. Then
\[
 \mathbb{E}(p1_Dp)=\sum_{g\in\Gamma}|p_g|^2\sigma_g(1_D)
 \geq |p_e|^2\sigma_e(1_D)=\tau(p)^2 1_D.
\]
To justify the first identity, let $p_F$ be the finite Fourier sums of $p$.
They converge to $p$ in $L^2(L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma)$, so $p_F1_Dp_F^*$ converges to
$p1_Dp$ in $L^1(L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma)$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. Apply the $L^1$-contractive
expectation and note that the series on the right converges in
operator norm, since $\sum_{g\in \Gamma}|p_g|^2=\tau(p)$.
If this expectation were scalar, trace preservation would imply that it equals
$\tau(p)\nu(D)1$, contrary to the lower bound on $D$.
Finally, an equality ${\mathcal P}=B\rtimes\Lambda$ in the canonical
embedding would force $\Lambda=\Gamma$, since $L(\Gamma)\subseteq{\mathcal P}$,
and $B={\mathbb C}1$, since ${\mathcal P}\cap L^\infty(X,\nu)={\mathbb C}1$. This contradicts
$\mathbb{E}({\mathcal P})\ne{\mathbb C}1$.

label: ex:relative-mixing-needed
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:relative-mixing-needed}
Let
$\Gamma={\mathbb F}_2$ be the free group on two generators, denoted $a$ and $b$.
Let $X=\{\pm1\}^{\Gamma}$ be equipped with the standard symmetric product measure $\nu$ and let $\Gamma$ act on $(X,\nu)$ by shifts.
 Write
$r_h(x)=x_h$ for $h\in\Gamma$, $x \in X$, so that $r_h \in L^\infty(X,\nu)$.
Then $\sigma_s(r_h)=r_{sh}$ for $s,h\in\Gamma$. For $h\in\Gamma$, let
$c_h=hah^{-1}$ and $q_h=r_hu_{c_h}\inL^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma$.
Let ${\mathcal P}=W^*(q_h\mid h\in\Gamma)\subseteqL^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma$. Then ${\mathcal P}$ is $\Gamma$-invariant. Indeed, for $s,h \in \Gamma$ we have
\[
u_s q_h u_s^*
=
u_s r_h u_{c_h}u_s^*
=
\sigma_s(r_h)u_{s c_hs^{-1}}
=
r_{sh}u_{(sh)a(sh)^{-1}}
=
q_{sh}.
\]
Let
$B={\mathcal P}\cap L^\infty(X,\nu)$. Then $B\neq\mathbb C1$. Indeed, for every $h\in\Gamma$, $c_h=c_{ha}$, so
$r_hr_{ha}=q_hq_{ha}^*\in B$.
This function is nonscalar.
We now show that ${\mathcal P}$ is not of the form $B\rtimes N$. Suppose, to the contrary, that
${\mathcal P}=B\rtimes N$
for some normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$. Since
$q_e=r_eu_a\in{\mathcal P}$
has Fourier support at $a$, we must have $a\in N$. Hence
$u_a\in B\rtimes N={\mathcal P}$.
Therefore $r_e=q_eu_a^*\in{\mathcal P}\capL^\infty(X,\nu)=B$.
We shall see that this is impossible, using the identification
$L^\infty(X,\nu)\rtimes\Gamma\cong L((\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)\rtimes\Gamma)$.
Under this identification, for every $h\in\Gamma$, $r_hu_{c_h}$ is the canonical unitary associated with the group element
$(\delta_h,c_h)$, where $\delta_h\in\bigoplus_\Gamma\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ has value $1$ at $h$ and $0$ elsewhere.
Let $K=\langle(\delta_h,c_h)\mid h\in\Gamma\rangle$, a subgroup of
$(\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)\rtimes\Gamma$. Then
${\mathcal P}=L(K)$,
and, since $B={\mathcal P}\capL^\infty(X,\nu)$, this identification gives $B=L\left(K\cap\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\right)$. Define a homomorphism $\chi$ from
$(\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)\rtimes\Gamma$ to $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$
by $\chi(\eta,g)=|\eta|+\operatorname{exp}_a(g)\pmod2$ for
$\eta\in\bigoplus_{\Gamma}\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ and $g\in\Gamma$. Here $|\eta|$ denotes the number of nonzero coordinates of $\eta$, and $\operatorname{exp}_a(g)$ is the $a$-exponent sum of $g$, namely the image of $g$ under the surjective homomorphism $\Gamma\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ sending $a$ to $1$ and $b$ to $0$. For every generator $(\delta_h,c_h)$ of $K$, we have
$|\delta_h|=1$, and
$\operatorname{exp}_a(c_h)=1$,
and hence $\chi(\delta_h,c_h)=0$.
Thus,
$K\subseteq\ker\chi$. But
$\chi(\delta_e,e)=1$, so 
$(\delta_e,e)\notin K$.
Equivalently,
$r_e\notin B$.
This contradicts the conclusion above. Hence ${\mathcal P}\neq B\rtimes N$ for every normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$.

Finally, we show explicitly that relative weak mixing over $B$ fails. Since
$c_e=c_{a^n}=a$
for every $n\ge1$, we have $q_e q_{a^n}^*
=
r_e r_{a^n}\in B$.
Moreover, from the description of $B$ above,
$\mathbb{E}_B(r_e)=0$. But
$\sigma_{a^n}(r_e)=r_{a^n}$. Therefore,
$\mathbb{E}_B\bigl(r_e^*\sigma_{a^n}(r_e)\bigr) = \mathbb{E}_B(r_e r_{a^n}) = r_e r_{a^n}.$
These functions have $L^2$ norm $1$ for every $n\ge1$, so $\sigma_a$ is not weakly mixing relative to $B$.

label: rem:bernoulli-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:bernoulli-scope}
Suppose that a compact second countable group $K$ acts non-trivially on $(X,\nu)$ by transformations $\kappa_k$, $k\in K$, which preserve $\nu$.
Assume that this action commutes with the p.m.p.\ action of $\Gamma$ and that its Koopman representation is strongly continuous. Then
$B=L^\infty(X,\nu)^K$ is a proper $\Gamma$-factor. If $\sigma_g$ is ergodic for a fixed $g\in\Gamma$, then $\sigma_g$ cannot be weakly mixing relative to $B$.

To see this, let $\pi$ denote the factor map from $X$ to $Y$ representing $B$, and let
$\lambda=\nu\times_Y\nu$ (see Remark  
    \IfBooleanTF{remark: relative weak mixing for diagonal action wrt a coordinate factor}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   for the notation used). For $k\in K$, let
$\lambda_k=(\mathrm{id},\kappa_k)_*\nu$. Haar averaging over $K$ yields the conditional
expectation onto $B$, and hence, for $f,h\in L^\infty(X,\nu)$,
\[
 \int_K\int_{X\times X} f(x)h(x')d\lambda_k(x,x')dk
 =\int_X f \mathbb{E}_B(h)d\nu
 =\int_{X\times X}f(x)h(x')d\lambda(x,x').
\]
Thus, $\lambda=\int_K\lambda_kdk$. Every $\lambda_k$ is invariant under
$\sigma_g\times\sigma_g$ ($k\in K$, $g \in \Gamma$), since $\kappa_k$ commutes with $\sigma_g$.
If $\sigma_g$ were weakly mixing relative to $B$, then $\lambda$ would be
an ergodic invariant probability measure, by
Remark~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{remark: relative weak mixing for diagonal action wrt a coordinate factor}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  .
Ergodic invariant probability measures are extreme among invariant
probability measures, so this decomposition gives $\lambda_k=\lambda$
for Haar almost every $k\in K$. For each $f\in L^{\infty}(X,\nu)$, the function
$k\mapsto\int_X f(x)\overline{f(\kappa_kx)}d\nu(x)$ is continuous by strong continuity of the Koopman representation. Its
almost everywhere constant value must therefore also be its value at
the identity. It follows that
\[
 \|f\|_2^2
 =\int_{X\times X}f(x)\overline{f(x')}d\lambda(x,x')
 =\|\mathbb{E}_B(f)\|_2^2.
\]
As $\mathbb{E}_B$ acts as an orthogonal projection on $L^2(X,\nu)$, this forces every
bounded $f$ to belong to $B$, contradicting properness.

In particular, this obstruction applies to Bernoulli shifts whose base admits a
non-trivial compact group of transformations preserving the base measure, including
the symmetric two-point base and, more generally, a compact group equipped with Haar measure.

\label{thm:gen}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group with the ECI property, and let $\sigma$
be a trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on $(Q,\tau_Q)$. Let
${\mathcal P}\subseteq Q\rtimes\Gamma$ be a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra, and let

label: eq:L1A
title: Proof
body_md:
Equivariance of $\mathbb{E}$ implies that $B$ is $\Gamma$-invariant. Fix $x\in{\mathcal P}$
with $\|x\|_\infty\le1$ and write $f_g=\mathbb{E}(xu_g^*)$ for $g\in\Gamma$.
We have $f_e\in B$. Fix $t_0\neq e$ and $\epsilon>0$. Choose a finite set
$F\subseteq\Gamma$ containing $e$ and $t_0$ such that $\|x-x_F\|_2<\epsilon$,
where $x_F=\sum_{g\in F}f_gu_g$, and let $F_1=F\cap C_\Gamma(t_0)$.
By ECI, there is $n_0\in{\mathbb N}$ such that
$t_0^n(F\setminus F_1)t_0^{-n}\cap F=\varnothing$ for every $n\ge n_0$.
For such $n$, let $c_n=\mathbb{E}(u_{t_0}^nxu_{t_0}^{-n}x^*)$.
Since ${\mathcal P}$ is invariant, $c_n\in B$ and $\|c_n\|_\infty\le1$.
Multiplying the finite Fourier sums gives
\[
 \mathbb{E}(u_{t_0}^nx_Fu_{t_0}^{-n}x_F^*)
 =\sum_{g\in F_1}\sigma_{t_0}^n(f_g)f_g^*.
\]
By equation~\eqref{eq:basic}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L1A}
 \left\|c_n-\sum_{g\in F_1}\sigma_{t_0}^n(f_g)f_g^*\right\|_1
 \le\|x-x_F\|_2\|x\|_2+\|x_F\|_2\|x-x_F\|_2<2\epsilon.
\end{equation}

Let $\xi\in Q$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}_B(\xi)=0$ and $\|\xi\|_\infty\le1$.
Apply the functional $a\mapsto\tau_Q(\xi^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi)a)$, whose norm on
$L^1(Q,\tau_Q)$ is at most one, to equation~\eqref{eq:L1A}.
Since $c_n\in B$ and $\|c_n\|_2\le1$, we have
\[
 |\tau_Q(\xi^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi)c_n)|
 =|\tau_Q(c_n\mathbb{E}_B(\xi^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi)))|
 \le\|\mathbb{E}_B(\xi^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi))\|_2.
\]
Relative weak mixing and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality show that the Ces\'aro averages of these
absolute values tend to zero. For each term in the finite sum, traciality gives
\[
 \tau_Q(\xi^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi)\sigma_{t_0}^n(f_g)f_g^*)
 =\tau_Q((\xi f_g)^*\sigma_{t_0}^n(\xi f_g)).
\]
By the mean ergodic theorem, the Ces\'aro averages on the right converge to the
squared norm of the orthogonal projection of $\xi f_g$ onto the invariant vectors
in $L^2(Q,\tau_Q)$. This limit is nonnegative and at least
$|\tau_Q(\xi f_g)|^2$, since the invariant subspace contains the constants.
Averaging the scalar inequality obtained from equation~\eqref{eq:L1A} and passing
to the limit therefore gives
$\sum_{g\in F_1}|\tau_Q(\xi f_g)|^2\le2\epsilon$.
Since $t_0\in F_1$ and $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, $\tau_Q(\xi f_{t_0})=0$.
By scaling, this holds for every $\xi\in Q$ with $\mathbb{E}_B(\xi)=0$.
Taking $\xi=(f_{t_0}-\mathbb{E}_B(f_{t_0}))^*$ gives
$\|f_{t_0}-\mathbb{E}_B(f_{t_0})\|_2^2=0$, so $f_{t_0}\in B$.
As $t_0\neq e$ was arbitrary, every Fourier coefficient of $x$ belongs to $B$,
and hence $x\in B\rtimes\Gamma$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tensor-center-valued-character}
Let ${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimesL^\infty(X,\nu)$ be a von Neumann
subalgebra such that $Z({\mathcal P})\subseteq\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}L^\infty(X,\nu)$, and write
$Z({\mathcal P})=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B$ for a von Neumann subalgebra $B\subseteqL^\infty(X,\nu)$.
Then $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)=1\otimes\mathbb{E}_B(f)$ for
all $f\inL^\infty(X,\nu)$. In particular, if ${\mathcal P}$ is a factor, then
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)=\nu(f)1$. If ${\mathcal P}$ is
$\Gamma$-invariant, then $B$ is $\Gamma$-invariant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $f\inL^\infty(X,\nu)$ and $x\in{\mathcal P}$, centrality of $1\otimes f$ and bimodularity of $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ give
\[
 x\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)
 =\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(x(1\otimes f))
 =\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}((1\otimes f)x)
 =\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)x.
\]
Thus, $\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)=1\otimes b_f$ for some $b_f\in B$.
For every $b\in B$, trace preservation gives
$\nu(b^*b_f) =\tau\bigl((1\otimes b)^*\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1\otimes f)\bigr) =\nu(b^*f)$.
This characterizes $b_f=\mathbb{E}_B(f)$. The factor assertion follows
by taking $B={\mathbb C}1$. If ${\mathcal P}$ is invariant, then $\theta_s$ preserves
$Z({\mathcal P})=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B$, so $\sigma_s(B)=B$ for every $s\in\Gamma$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $g\neq e$ and write
$x=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(\lambda_g\otimes1)
  =\sum_{t\in\Gamma}\lambda_t\otimes f_t$.
Equivariance gives $\theta_g(x)=x$, and comparison of Fourier
coefficients yields $f_{gtg^{-1}}=\sigma_g(f_t)$ for every $t\in\Gamma$.
On an infinite orbit under conjugation by $g$, all coefficients have
the same $L^2$ norm. Since $\sum_t\|f_t\|_2^2=\|x\|_2^2<\infty$,
these coefficients vanish. On an orbit of finite length $m$,
$\sigma_g^m(f_t)=f_t$. Every positive power of a weakly mixing
transformation is ergodic, so $f_t$ is scalar. Indeed, a nonzero
mean-zero function fixed by $\sigma_g^m$ would generate a nonzero
finite-dimensional invariant subspace under $\sigma_g$, contradicting
weak mixing. Thus, every Fourier coefficient of $x$ is scalar, and
$x\in L^2(L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1)$. As $x$ is bounded, it belongs to
$L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1$. The case $g=e$ follows from
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(1)=1$.

                                                               
                                           
The $L^2$-continuity of
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ shows that it preserves $L^2(L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1)$. For a bounded element of $L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1$, its expectation
is bounded as well, so it belongs to $L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1$. 
This proves
the first containment. Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:commuting-square}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  , applied to
${\mathcal P}$ and $L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1$, now gives the second containment.

label: thm:tensor-center-in-A
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:tensor-center-in-A}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group with the ISR property. Let
$\Gamma\curvearrowright(X,\nu)$ be a p.m.p.~action which is pointwise weakly mixing relative to every proper $\Gamma$-factor of $L^\infty(X,\nu)$, including the
trivial factor. Let ${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes L^\infty(X,\nu)$ be a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann
subalgebra such that $Z({\mathcal P})\subseteq\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}L^\infty(X,\nu)$, i.e.~$Z({\mathcal P})=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B$ for a
$\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra $B\subseteqL^\infty(X,\nu)$. Then there exists a normal subgroup
$N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$ such that ${\mathcal P}=L(N)\bar\otimes B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $L^\infty(X,\nu)={\mathbb C}1$, the assertion follows directly from the ISR property. Otherwise the
trivial factor is proper, so $\sigma$ is pointwise weakly mixing.
Set ${\mathcal R}=\mathbb{E}_{L(\Gamma)}({\mathcal P})$. By
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:tensor-group-expectation}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  , ${\mathcal R}\subseteq{\mathcal P}$.
Since ${\mathcal R}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1$,
we have ${\mathcal R}\subseteq{\mathcal P}\cap(L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1)$. Conversely, if $x\in{\mathcal P}\cap(L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1)$, then
$\mathbb{E}_{L(\Gamma)}(x)=x$, and hence $x\in {\mathcal R}$. Thus, ${\mathcal R}={\mathcal P}\cap(L(\Gamma)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1)$. In particular,
${\mathcal R}$ is a $\Gamma$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra of $L(\Gamma)$, and by the ISR property ${\mathcal R}=L(N)$
for some normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq\Gamma$.

We claim that ${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes B$. By Remark~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{rem:tensor-cs}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  , ${\mathcal P}$ forms a
commuting square with $\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}L^\infty(X,\nu)$ and ${\mathcal P}\cap(\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}L^\infty(X,\nu))=\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B$. If $B=L^\infty(X,\nu)$ there is
nothing to prove. Otherwise $B$ is a proper $\Gamma$-factor, $\sigma$ is pointwise weakly mixing relative
to $B$ and the claim follows from Corollary~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{cor:cs-tensor}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  .

Next, we claim that ${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(N)\bar\otimes B$. Let $t\notin N$. First note that
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(\lambda_t\otimes1)=0$. Indeed, for every $z\in{\mathcal P}$ we have
$\langle\lambda_t\otimes1,z\rangle=\langle\lambda_t\otimes1,\mathbb{E}_{L(\Gamma)}(z)\rangle=0$, since
$\mathbb{E}_{L(\Gamma)}(z)\in {\mathcal R}=L(N)$ and $\lambda_t\perp L(N)$. Consequently, for every $b\in B$,
bimodularity gives
$\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(\lambda_t\otimes b)=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(\lambda_t\otimes1)(1\otimes b)=0$, because
$1\otimes b\in Z({\mathcal P})\subseteq{\mathcal P}$. Now let $x=\sum_{s\in\Gamma}\lambda_s\otimes f_s\in{\mathcal P}$. By the
previous claim $f_t\in B$, and therefore
$\|f_t\|_2^2=\langle x,\lambda_t\otimes f_t\rangle=\langle x,\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal P}}(\lambda_t\otimes f_t)\rangle=0$.
Thus, every Fourier coefficient of $x$ outside $N$ vanishes, which proves the claim.

Finally, $L(N)\bar{\otimes}\mathbb{C}1={\mathcal R}\subseteq{\mathcal P}$ and $\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes} B=Z({\mathcal P})\subseteq{\mathcal P}$, so
$L(N)\bar\otimes B\subseteq{\mathcal P}$. Together with the previous claim, we see that ${\mathcal P}=L(N)\bar\otimes B$.

label: prop:insideamenradtensor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:insideamenradtensor}
Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group, let $(Q,\tau_Q)$ be a von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial state and let
$\sigma$ be a trace-preserving action of $\Gamma$ on $(Q,\tau_Q)$. Let
$M=L(\Gamma)\bar\otimes Q$ and let $\theta$ be again the diagonal action of $\Gamma$ on $M$, given by
$\theta_s(\lambda_t\otimes a)=\lambda_{sts^{-1}}\otimes\sigma_s(a)$
for $s,t\in\Gamma$ and $a\in Q$.
If ${\mathcal P}\subseteq M$ is an amenable von Neumann subalgebra such that
$\theta_s({\mathcal P})={\mathcal P}$ for every $s\in\Gamma$, then
${\mathcal P}\subseteq L(\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma))\bar\otimes Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By our standing assumption, $Q$ has separable predual.
Let $\widetilde{M}=M\rtimes_\theta\Gamma$, and denote by $v_s$, $s\in\Gamma$, the canonical
unitaries implementing the action inside $\widetilde{M}$, so that  $v_sxv_s^*=\theta_s(x)$ for every $x\in M$, $s \in \Gamma$. Hence when we view ${\mathcal P}$ inside $\widetilde{M}$, the assumption
$\theta_s({\mathcal P})={\mathcal P}$ becomes $v_s{\mathcal P} v_s^*={\mathcal P}$. Write $u_t=\lambda_t\otimes1\in M$, $t \in \Gamma$. Then
$v_su_tv_s^*=u_{sts^{-1}}$.

The automorphism action is now represented as conjugation, while the Fourier support we want to control
is still the support in the $u_t$-coordinate. Apply the construction of  Subsection~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{subsec:boundary-rep}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  
with $Z=\partial_F\Gamma$. By minimality, every $x_0\in\partial_F\Gamma$
has a dense orbit, so the multiplication operators $m_f$ defined there give a faithful
representation of $C(\partial_F\Gamma)$ on $L^2(\widetilde M)$.
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:boundary-covariance}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   gives
$u_tm_fu_t^*=m_{t\cdot f}$ and $v_sm_fv_s^*=m_{s\cdot f}$ for all $s,t\in\Gamma$, $f \in C(\partial_F\Gamma)$.

Let $\widetilde\tau$ be the canonical trace on $\widetilde M$. Since $Q$
has separable predual and $\Gamma$ is countable, $\widetilde M$ also has
separable predual. Let
$\mathcal H=\operatorname{Hype}_{\widetilde\tau}({\mathcal P})$ be the set of states
$\varphi$ on $\mathbb B(L^2(\widetilde M))$ satisfying
$\varphi|_{\widetilde M}=\widetilde\tau$ and $\varphi(aT)=\varphi(Ta)$ for all $a\in{\mathcal P}$ and $T\in\mathbb B(L^2(\widetilde M))$.
By \cite[Proposition~2.4]{amrutam2025amenable}, $\mathcal H$ is nonempty.
These are weak$^*$-closed affine conditions
on the state space, so $\mathcal H$ is compact and convex. It is invariant
under the action given by $(s\cdot\varphi)(T)=\varphi(v_s^*Tv_s)$ ($s\in\Gamma$, $\varphi\in\mathcal H$, $T\in\mathbb B(L^2(\widetilde M))$) because $v_s$ normalises ${\mathcal P}$ and $\widetilde\tau$ is a trace.
Restriction to the represented copy of $C(\partial_F\Gamma)$ is a
continuous affine map, and Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:boundary-covariance}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   makes it
$\Gamma$-equivariant. Its image
$\mathcal K=\{\varphi|_{C(\partial_F\Gamma)}\mid\varphi\in\mathcal H\}\subseteq\operatorname{Prob}(\partial_F\Gamma)$
is therefore nonempty, compact, convex and $\Gamma$-invariant. Hence it equals
$\operatorname{Prob}(\partial_F\Gamma)$ (see for example \cite[Section~2]{amrutam2025amenable}).

\begin{comment}
                                             
                                                          
                                                                       
                                                           
                                                                     
                                                                      
                                                                        
                                                        
                                                   
\end{comment}

Fix $t_0\in\Gamma\setminus\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma)$. Since
$\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma)=\ker(\Gamma\curvearrowright\partial_F\Gamma)$, we may choose $x\in \partial_F\Gamma$ such
that $t_0x\neq x$. Choose $f\in C(\partial_F\Gamma)$ with $0\leq f\leq1$, $f(x)=1$, and $f(t_0x)=0$. By the
previous paragraph we can select
$\varphi\in\operatorname{Hype}_{\widetilde\tau}({\mathcal P})$ such that $\varphi|_{C(\partial_F\Gamma)}=\delta_x$.
Then $C(\partial_F\Gamma)$ is contained in the multiplicative domain of $\varphi$.
Let $a\in{\mathcal P}$ and $b\in Q$. Write $f'=t_0^{-1}\cdot f$, so that $u_{t_0}^*(1\otimes b)=(1\otimes b)u_{t_0}^*$,
$u_{t_0}^*m_f=m_{f'}u_{t_0}^*$ and $u_{t_0}m_{f'}u_{t_0}^*=m_f$. Note that
$0\le f'\le1$,
$\varphi(f')=f'(x)=f(t_0x)=0$, and  $C(\partial_F\Gamma)$ commutes with
$\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}Q$ in $\mathbb{B}(L^2(\widetilde{M}))$ (both act
diagonally in the two $\ell^2(\Gamma)$-coordinates, the former by scalars on
each fibre). Using the multiplicative-domain identities and ${\mathcal P}$-centrality, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\widetilde\tau\bigl(a u_{t_0}^*(1\otimes b)\bigr)
 &=\varphi\bigl(a u_{t_0}^*(1\otimes b)\bigr) =\varphi\bigl(a u_{t_0}^*(1\otimes b)m_f\bigr)\\
 &=\varphi\bigl(u_{t_0}^*(1\otimes b)m_f a\bigr) =\varphi\bigl(m_{f'}(1\otimes b)u_{t_0}^*a\bigr) \\&=\varphi(m_{f'})\varphi\bigl((1\otimes b)u_{t_0}^*a\bigr)=0.
\end{align*}
Here the second equality uses $f(x)=1$, the third uses $a\in{\mathcal P}$,
the fourth uses covariance and commutation with $\mathbb{C}1\bar{\otimes}Q$, and the
last uses $f'(x)=0$.

                                                                                                      
Let $\mathbb{E}_Q$ denote the canonical conditional expectation from $M$ onto $\mathbb{C}1\bar\otimes Q$, identified with $Q$.
The last identity gives
$\tau_Q(b\mathbb{E}_Q(au_{t_0}^*))=0$ for every $b\in Q$. Hence
$\mathbb{E}_Q(au_{t_0}^*)=0$.
Since $t_0\notin\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma)$ was arbitrary, all Fourier coefficients of $a$ outside
$\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma)$ vanish. Thus, $a\in L(\operatorname{Rad}(\Gamma))\bar\otimes Q$.

Since $a\in{\mathcal P}$ was arbitrary, this proves the assertion.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\epsilon$ be the augmentation homomorphism from $V$ to $\mathbb Z$, given by
$\epsilon(\sum_s c_ss)=\sum_s c_s$, and let $I=\ker\epsilon$.
Choose a free generator $s_1$ and let $\phi$ be the homomorphism from ${\mathbb F}_n$ to $\mathbb Z$ that sends
$s_1$ to $1$ and every other free generator to $0$. Define the homomorphism $D$ from $V\times{\mathbb F}_n$ to $\mathbb Z$ by $D(v,s)=\epsilon(v)-\phi(s)$. Its kernel is $H=\{(\phi(s)e+x,s)\mid x\in I,s\in{\mathbb F}_n\}$,
where $e$ denotes the basis element of $V$ at the group identity.
Since $\epsilon(gv)=\epsilon(v)$ and
$\phi(gsg^{-1})=\phi(s)$, the kernel is invariant under the given
diagonal action. Its intersection with $V$ is $I$, which is nonzero
because $s_1-e\in I$ and is proper because $\epsilon(e)=1$.

The projection of $H$ to ${\mathbb F}_n$ is onto. Its projection to $V$ is also
onto, since for $v\in V$ we can choose $s$ with $\phi(s)=\epsilon(v)$.
But $(0,s_1)\notin H$. If $H=H_1\times H_2$, the two projections would
force $H_1=V$ and $H_2={\mathbb F}_n$, contradicting this last fact. This proves (3).

Suppose that $L(H)=B_2\bar\otimes B_1$. For each $(v,s)\in H$, the unitary
$\lambda_s\otimes\lambda_v$ belongs to $B_2\bar\otimes B_1$.
Applying the normal slice maps defined by
$z\mapsto\tau_{{\mathbb F}_n}(\lambda_s^*z)$ and
$z\mapsto\tau_V(\lambda_v^*z)$ gives $\lambda_v\in B_1$ and $\lambda_s\in B_2$.
Surjectivity of the two group projections therefore implies
$B_1=L(V)$ and $B_2=L({\mathbb F}_n)$. It follows that
$\lambda_{(0,s_1)}\in L(H)$, which is impossible because the Fourier expansion of every
element of $L(H)$ is supported in $H$. This proves (4).

label: lem:disjointization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:disjointization}
Let $P_1,\ldots,P_k\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$, and let $D\subseteq X$ be a Borel set
such that $P_1(x),\ldots,P_k(x)$ are pairwise distinct for every $x\in D$.
If $0\leq a<\nu(D)$, then there are pairwise disjoint Borel sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_M\subseteq D$ such that
$\nu(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_M)>a$ and, for every $r=1, \ldots,M$, the sets
$P_1(A_r),\ldots,P_k(A_r)$ are pairwise disjoint.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Because $X$ is a standard Borel space, there is a countable Boolean algebra
$\mathcal A$ of Borel sets which separates points. For example, after
identifying $X$ with a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, one may pull back the algebra
of finite unions of intervals with rational endpoints.

Fix $x\in D$. Since $P_1(x),\ldots,P_k(x)$ are distinct, for every pair of
these points choose a member of $\mathcal A$ which contains one and not the
other. The finitely many chosen sets generate a finite Boolean algebra, and
the points $P_1(x),\ldots,P_k(x)$ lie in distinct atoms of that finite
algebra.                                                                
               
Hence there exist pairwise disjoint sets
$V_1,\ldots,V_k\in\mathcal A$ with $P_i(x)\in V_i$ for every $i=1, \ldots,k$.

For every pairwise disjoint $k$-tuple
$\mathbf V=(V_1,\ldots,V_k)$ from $\mathcal A$, let
 $U_{\mathbf V}=D\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^k P_i^{-1}(V_i)$.
There are only countably many such tuples, these sets cover $D$, and
$P_i(U_{\mathbf V})\subseteq V_i$; therefore the images of each
$U_{\mathbf V}$ are pairwise disjoint Borel sets. Enumerate the nonempty sets in this
cover as $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ and let $B_1=U_1$ and
$B_r=U_r\setminus\bigcup_{j<r}U_j$ for $r\geq2$.
Then $D=\bigsqcup_{r\geq1}B_r$, and the images
$P_1(B_r),\ldots,P_k(B_r)$ are pairwise disjoint for every $r$. Since
$\nu(\bigcup_{r=1}^N B_r)\to\nu(D)>a$, a sufficiently large finite initial
union has measure greater than $a$. Discarding its null members gives the
required sets.

label: lem:local-modification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-modification}
Let $R\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let
$\mathcal C$ be a finite family of Borel sets. There is an involution
$P\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\text{supp}(P)=D$ modulo null sets;
\item $P$ preserves every member of the finite Boolean algebra generated by
\[
 \{D\}\cup\mathcal C
 \cup\{R(C)\mid C\in\mathcal C\}
 \cup\{R^{-1}(C)\mid C\in\mathcal C\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, for both $R_+=RP$ and $R_-=PR$ one has
 $R_\pm(C)=R(C)$,
 $R_\pm^{-1}(C)=R^{-1}(C)$ for every $C\in\mathcal C$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The displayed family is finite, hence it generates a finite Boolean algebra.
Atoms of this algebra arise as intersections obtained by choosing, for each generator, either the set itself or its complement. Since $D$ is one of the generators, every atom
is either contained in $D$ or disjoint from $D$.

Let $E$ be a positive-measure atom contained in $D$. The restriction of
$\nu$ to $E$ is nonatomic, so we can choose a Borel partition
$E=E^0\sqcup E^1$ with $\nu(E^0)=\nu(E^1)$. The two standard nonatomic
finite measure spaces $E^0$ and $E^1$ are measure-isomorphic; this follows,
for example, from the standard isomorphism theorem recalled in
\cite[Section~1(A)]{kechris2010global}. Choose a measure-preserving Borel
isomorphism $\psi_E$ from $E^0$ to $E^1$ modulo null sets. Define $P$ to be
$\psi_E$ on each $E^0$, $\psi_E^{-1}$ on each $E^1$, and the identity outside the
union of the positive-measure atoms contained in $D$. Then $P$ is a
measure-preserving involution which has no fixed point on $D$ modulo null
sets.                                                                 
                                                                        
                                         
Furthermore, it preserves every atom, hence
every member, of the finite Boolean algebra in question. In particular, for
$C\in\mathcal C$, we have
$ P(C)=C$, $P(R(C))=R(C)$, $P(R^{-1}(C))=R^{-1}(C)$.
Hence $R_+(C)=R(P(C))=R(C)$ and
$R_+^{-1}(C)=P(R^{-1}(C))=R^{-1}(C)$, and likewise
$R_-(C)=P(R(C))=R(C)$ and $R_-^{-1}(C)=R^{-1}(P(C))=R^{-1}(C)$.
The claim follows.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a maximal $i_0\in \{0, \ldots,n-1\}$ such that
$ v_{i_0+1}=b^\varepsilon v_{i_0}$ for some $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$.
This corresponds to the leftmost occurrence of $b^{\pm1}$ in $v$.
                         
Consequently, every letter which appears before this
selected occurrence is $a$ or $a^{-1}$. Let
 $F=A\cap\text{Fix}(v^{T,S})$, and
 $D=v_{i_0}^{T,S}(F)$.
 
If $\nu(F)=0$, it suffices to take $S'=S$. Suppose that $\nu(F)>0$, and apply
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:local-modification}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to $S$, $D$, and $\mathcal C$. Let $P$
be the resulting involution with support $D$.
Note that $D\subseteq v_{i_0}^{T,S}(A)$, so that $D$ is disjoint from
$v_i^{T,S}(A)$ for every $i<n$ with $i\neq i_0$.

Suppose first that $\varepsilon=1$ and set $S'=SP$. We first claim that,
for $x\in A$ and $0\leq i\leq i_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:path-before-selected-positive}
 v_i^{T,S'}(x)=v_i^{T,S}(x).
\end{equation}
We argue by induction on $i$. For $i=0$ both sides equal $x$. Assume
the equality holds at some $i<i_0$,
and let $z=v_i^{T,S'}(x)=v_i^{T,S}(x)$. If the next letter appearing on the left is $a^{\pm1}$, the
next step is unchanged. If it is $b$, then
$S'(z)=S(Pz)=S(z)$ because
$z\in v_i^{T,S}(A)$ and this set is disjoint from
$D\subseteq v_{i_0}^{T,S}(A)$. If the next letter is $b^{-1}$, then
$v_{i+1}^{T,S'}(x)=S'^{-1}(z)=P(S^{-1}z)=P(v_{i+1}^{T,S}(x))$.
When $i+1<i_0$, the point $v_{i+1}^{T,S}(x)$ lies outside $D$ by the same
pairwise disjointness. The only remaining possibility is $i+1=i_0$; but
then the letter immediately to the right of the selected $b$ would be
$b^{-1}$, contradicting the fact that $v$ is reduced. Hence the last expression is
$S^{-1}z$, and equation~\eqref{eq:path-before-selected-positive} follows.

Write $v=qb^{\varepsilon}v_{i_0}$, where
$q=\ell_1\cdots\ell_{n-i_0-1}$. By the maximality of $i_0$, the word $q$
involves only letters $a^{\pm1}$, so that $q^{T,S'}=q^{T,S}=T^{m}$ for some $m\in{\mathbb Z}$;
in particular this transformation does not depend on the second generator.
                     

Take $x\in F$ and let $y=v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)$. Note that $y\in D$, so that
$P(y)\neq y$. Since $S$ is injective, it follows that
$S'(y)=S(P(y))\neq S(y)$. By equation~\eqref{eq:path-before-selected-positive} we
have $v_{i_0}^{T,S'}(x)=y$, and therefore
$v^{T,S'}(x) =q^{T,S}\bigl(S'(y)\bigr) \neq q^{T,S}\bigl(S(y)\bigr) =v^{T,S}(x) =x$.

If $x\in A\setminus F$, then $v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)\notin D$, since
$D=v_{i_0}^{T,S}(F)$. Hence
$P\bigl(v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)\bigr)=v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)$.
By equation~\eqref{eq:path-before-selected-positive},
$v_{i_0}^{T,S'}(x)=v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)$, and therefore
$S'\bigl(v_{i_0}^{T,S'}(x)\bigr) = S\bigl(P(v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x))\bigr) = S\bigl(v_{i_0}^{T,S}(x)\bigr)$.
Since the remaining letters of $v$ are those of $q$, it follows that
$v^{T,S'}(x)=v^{T,S}(x)\neq x$. This proves (ii) when $\varepsilon=1$.

The case $\varepsilon=-1$ reduces to the case $\varepsilon=1$ by replacing
the second generator $b$ with $b^{-1}$ and $S$ with $S^{-1}$. More precisely,
let $\sigma$ be the automorphism of ${\mathbb F}_2$ determined by setting $\sigma(a)=a$ and
$\sigma(b)=b^{-1}$, and let $\widehat S=S^{-1}$ and $w=\sigma(v)$. Then $w^{T,\widehat{S}}=v^{T,S}$ and
$w_i^{T,\widehat{S}}=v_i^{T,S}$ for $0\leq i < n$.
As $w$ is a reduced word of length $n$ in which $b^{\pm1}$ occurs, the
hypothesis on $A$ holds for $w$ and $\widehat S$. The leftmost occurrence
of $b^{\pm1}$ in $w$ is at the same place as in $v$ and has exponent $+1$,
and the sets $F$ and $D$ attached to $w$ and $\widehat S$ are the same as the ones
attached to $v$ and $S$. Finally, the finite family displayed in
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:local-modification}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   is the same for $\widehat S$ as for $S$,
because $\widehat S^{\pm1}(C)=S^{\mp1}(C)$; so the same involution $P$
occurs. The case already treated yields
$\widehat S'=\widehat S P=S^{-1}P$ with
$\nu\bigl(A\cap\text{Fix}(w^{T,\widehat S'})\bigr)=0$. Setting
 $S'=(\widehat S')^{-1}=PS$,
and noting that $w^{T,\widehat S'}=v^{T,S'}$ for the same reason as above, we
obtain $S'^{\pm1}(C)=S^{\pm1}(C)$ for every $C\in\mathcal C$ and
$\nu\bigl(A\cap\text{Fix}(v^{T,S'})\bigr)=0$.
Assertion (i) follows from the final claim of
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:local-modification}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  , applied to $R_+=SP$ when
$\varepsilon=1$ and to $R_-=PS$ when $\varepsilon=-1$.

label: prop:generic-second-generator
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:generic-second-generator}
Let $T\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ be aperiodic.
    
                                                              
                      
                  
Then the set of $S$ for which $\alpha^{T,S}$ is essentially free is comeager in
${\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$. If $T$ is ergodic, every such $\alpha^{T,S}$ is ergodic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ergodicity assertion is immediate since every $\alpha^{T,S}$-invariant set is
$T$-invariant.

For a non-trivial reduced word $v\in{\mathbb F}_2$ and $0<\epsilon\leq1$, let
${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)=\{S\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)\mid d_{\mathrm u}(v^{T,S},\mathrm{id})>1-\epsilon\}$.
By equation~\eqref{eq:du-fix}, $S$ belongs to ${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$ for every
$\epsilon$ if and only if $\nu(\text{Fix}(v^{T,S}))=0$.

We first prove that the sets ${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$ are open.
The word map $S\mapsto v^{T,S}$ is  continuous, since
${\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ is a topological group. Moreover, the map
$R\longmapsto d_{\mathrm u}(R,\mathrm{id})$
is lower semicontinuous; equivalently, for every
$c>0$, the set
$\{R\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)\mid d_{\mathrm u}(R,\mathrm{id})>c\}$
is  open; see \cite[Section~1(C), pp.~3--4]{kechris2010global}.
Consequently, ${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$ is  open.

We now prove by induction on the  length of $v$  that
${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$ is dense
for every non-trivial word $v$ and every $0<\epsilon\leq1$.

If $|v|=1$ and $v=a^{\pm1}$, then
$d_{\mathrm u}(v^{T,S},\mathrm{id})=1$ for every $S$ because $T$ is aperiodic, by
equation~\eqref{eq:du-fix}; hence ${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)={\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$. If
$v=b^{\pm1}$, density follows from the fact that aperiodic transformations
form a dense $G_\delta$ subset of ${\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$
\cite[Proposition~2.3]{kechris2010global}, since
$d_{\mathrm u}(S^{\pm1},\mathrm{id})=1$ for every aperiodic $S$.

Now fix $n\geq2$, assume the density assertion for every non-trivial  word
of length less than $n$, and let $v\in {\mathbb F}_2$ have length $n$. Let
${\mathcal N}$ be an arbitrary nonempty basic 
neighbourhood, so that 
\begin{equation} \label{def:N}{\mathcal N}=\bigl\{R\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)\mid 
   \nu\bigl(R(C_j)\triangle S_*(C_j)\bigr)<\kappa,1\leq j\leq q\bigr\}
\end{equation}
for some $S_*\in {\rm Aut}(X, \nu)$, $q \in {\mathbb N}$, Borel sets $C_1, \ldots,C_q$ in $X$ and $\kappa>0$. 
Since such sets form a basis for the weak topology, it
suffices to show that ${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)\cap{\mathcal N}\neq\varnothing$.
If $v\in\langle a\rangle$,
then $v^{T,S}$ is a nonzero power of the aperiodic transformation $T$ and has
null fixed-point set for every $S$. We may therefore assume that
$b^{\pm1}$ occurs in $v$.

By the induction hypothesis,
\[
 {\mathcal D}_{<n}
 =\bigcap_{\substack{u\neq e\\|u|<n}}
    \bigcap_{r\geq1}{\mathcal U}(u,1/r)
\]
is a dense $G_\delta$ set because it is a countable intersection of dense open
sets, and ${\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ is Polish, hence a Baire space. Choose
$S_0\in{\mathcal N}\cap{\mathcal D}_{<n}$, which is possible because ${\mathcal N}$ is nonempty
and open. By equation~\eqref{eq:du-fix}, for every non-trivial word $u$
with $|u|<n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dn-fix}
 \nu\bigl(\text{Fix}(u^{{T,S_0}})\bigr)=0.
\end{equation}

Write $v=\ell_1\cdots\ell_n$ and for $i=0, \ldots,n$ let $v_i$ be the terminal subwords
of $v$, as introduced before Proposition  
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:remove-fixed-points}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  . We
claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-points}
 v_0^{T,S_0}(x),v_1^{T,S_0}(x),\ldots,v_{n-1}^{T,S_0}(x)
\end{equation}
are pairwise distinct for almost every $x\in X$. Indeed, if $0\leq i<j<n$, then
$v_j=u_{j,i}v_i$, where
$u_{j,i}=\ell_{n-j+1}\cdots\ell_{n-i}$ is a non-trivial word of
length $j-i<n$. If
$v_j^{T,S_0}(x)=v_i^{T,S_0}(x)$ and
$y=v_i^{T,S_0}(x)$, then $u_{j,i}^{T,S_0}(y)=y$. The fixed-point set of
$u_{j,i}^{T,S_0}$ is null by equation~\eqref{eq:Dn-fix}; since
$v_i^{T,S_0}$ preserves measure, the set of such $x$ is null. There are only
finitely many pairs $(i,j)$, proving the claim.

Let $D_0\subseteq X$ be a conull Borel set on which the points in
equation~\eqref{eq:terminal-points} are pairwise distinct. Apply
Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:disjointization}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to
$v_0^{T,S_0},\ldots,v_{n-1}^{T,S_0}$ on $D_0$, with $a=1-\epsilon$. We obtain
pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_M$ such that
$\nu(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_M)>1-\epsilon$ and, for each $r=1, \ldots, M$, the sets
$v_0^{T,S_0}(A_r),\ldots,v_{n-1}^{T,S_0}(A_r)$ are pairwise disjoint. Let
$\eta=\nu(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_M)-(1-\epsilon)>0$ and
$\delta=\frac{\eta}{2M}$.

We shall now show that for each $r=1,\ldots,M$ there exist
$S_r\in {\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ and a finite collection
${\mathcal B}_r$ of pairwise disjoint Borel subsets of $A_r$ such that
the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $S_r\in{\mathcal N}$;
\item for every $p=1, \ldots, M, p\leq r$ and every $B\in{\mathcal B}_p$,
      $B\cap v^{T,S_r}(B)=\varnothing$;
\item for every $j=1,\ldots, M$, $j>r$ and $i=0,\ldots,n-1$,
      $v_i^{T,S_r}(A_j)=v_i^{T,S_0}(A_j)$;
\item $\displaystyle\sum_{B\in{\mathcal B}_p}\nu(B)\geq\nu(A_p)-\delta$
      for every $p=1, \ldots, M, p\leq r$.
\end{enumerate}
We construct these inductively, starting at $r=0$ with the chosen $S_0$ and the empty family ${\mathcal B}_0$.

Now let $r\in \{1,\ldots,M\}$, and suppose that $S_{r-1}$ and ${\mathcal B}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal B}_{r-1}$ have been constructed
so that (a)--(d) hold at stage $r-1$.
From (c) at stage $r-1$, applied to $j=r$, we see that
$v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(A_r)=v_i^{T,S_0}(A_r)$
for $0\leq i<n$,
so these are the original pairwise disjoint images of $A_r$; in
particular $S_{r-1}$, $A_r$ and $v$ satisfy the hypothesis of
Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:remove-fixed-points}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
  .

The next perturbation must preserve exactly three finite collections of
sets, namely the sets defining ${\mathcal N}$, the complete $v$-paths of the blocks
already chosen, and the complete $v$-paths of the sets which have not yet
been seen. Accordingly, consider the finite family
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal C_r={}&\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\} \cup\\
&\{v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(B)\mid p<r,B\in{\mathcal B}_p,0\leq i<n\} \cup\\
&\{v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(A_j)\mid j>r,0\leq i<n\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
                                                                    

Apply Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:remove-fixed-points}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to $S_{r-1}$, $A_r$, and
$\mathcal C_r$, and call the resulting transformation $S_r$;
thus, $S_r^{\pm1}(C)=S_{r-1}^{\pm1}(C)$ for every $C\in\mathcal C_r$,
and $\nu\bigl(A_r\cap\text{Fix}(v^{T,S_r})\bigr)=0$. 
If $\nu(A_r)\leq\delta$, let ${\mathcal B}_r=\varnothing$. If
$\nu(A_r)>\delta$, apply Lemma~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{lem:disjointization}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to
$\mathrm{id}$ and $v^{T,S_r}$ on the Borel set
$A_r\setminus\text{Fix}(v^{T,S_r})$, with $a=\nu(A_r)-\delta$.
Note that the conditions of the lemma are satisfied as
$\nu\bigl(A_r\setminus\text{Fix}(v^{T,S_r})\bigr)=\nu(A_r)>\nu(A_r)-\delta$,
and $\mathrm{id}(x)\neq v^{T,S_r}(x)$ for $x \in A_r\setminus\text{Fix}(v^{T,S_r})$.
We thus obtain a finite
family ${\mathcal B}_r$ of pairwise disjoint subsets of $A_r$ such that
$\sum_{B\in{\mathcal B}_r}\nu(B)>\nu(A_r)-\delta$ and
$B\cap v^{T,S_r}(B)=\varnothing$ for every $B\in{\mathcal B}_r$.

We shall now check that the conditions
(a)--(d) hold at stage $r$.

First check (a). Recall equation~\eqref{def:N}.
                                  
                                                                        
   
It is obvious that if $R,R'\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ satisfy
$R'(C_j)=R(C_j)$ for $1\leq j\leq q$, then $R\in{\mathcal N}$ if and only if
$R'\in{\mathcal N}$. Now $C_j\in\mathcal C_r$ for $1\leq j\leq q$, by the definition of
$\mathcal C_r$, and $S_r$ was obtained by applying
Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:remove-fixed-points}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to $S_{r-1}$ with the family
$\mathcal C_r$. Condition~(i) of that proposition, applied to $C=C_j$,
gives
$ S_r(C_j)=S_{r-1}(C_j)$ for $1\leq j\leq q$.
The induction hypothesis (a) at stage $r-1$ says that $S_{r-1}\in{\mathcal N}$.
By the previous paragraph, $S_r\in{\mathcal N}$, which is (a) at stage $r$.

To verify (b), let $p<r$ and $B\in{\mathcal B}_p$. The sets $v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(B)$, $0\leq i<n$,
belong to $\mathcal C_r$, so equation~\eqref{eq:path-sets-preserved} gives
$v_i^{T,S_r}(B)=v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(B)$ for $0\leq i\leq n$; taking $i=n$ yields
$v^{T,S_r}(B)=v^{T,S_{r-1}}(B)$, and (b) at stage $r-1$ gives
$B\cap v^{T,S_r}(B)=\varnothing$. For $p=r$ the assertion holds by the properties of ${\mathcal B}_r$ stated above.

For (c), let $j>r$. The sets $v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(A_j)$, $0\leq i<n$, also belong to
$\mathcal C_r$, so equation~\eqref{eq:path-sets-preserved}, together with (c) at
stage $r-1$, gives
$v_i^{T,S_r}(A_j)=v_i^{T,S_{r-1}}(A_j)=v_i^{T,S_0}(A_j)$ for $0\leq i<n$.

Finally, the families ${\mathcal B}_p$ with $p<r$ are unchanged, so (d) persists for
those $p$; and for $p=r$ this holds by the choice of ${\mathcal B}_r$.

This completes the inductive construction.

Note now that every point in every $B\in{\mathcal B}_r$ is moved by
$v^{T,S_M}$, because $B\cap v^{T,S_M}(B)=\varnothing$
by (b) at stage $M$. Since the sets $A_r$ are
pairwise disjoint, all the sets in the family ${\mathcal B}_1 \cup \cdots \cup {\mathcal B}_M$ are pairwise
disjoint. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \nu\bigl(\{x\mid v^{T,S_M}(x)\neq x\}\bigr)
 &\geq\sum_{r=1}^M\sum_{B\in{\mathcal B}_r}\nu(B)
 \geq\sum_{r=1}^M(\nu(A_r)-\delta)\\&=\nu(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_M)-M\delta
 =1-\epsilon+\frac{\eta}{2}>1-\epsilon.
\end{align*}
Hence $S_M\in{\mathcal N}\cap{\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$. Since ${\mathcal N}$ was arbitrary,
${\mathcal U}(v,\epsilon)$ is dense, and the induction on $|v|$ is complete.

Thus, every set ${\mathcal U}(v,1/r)$, with $v\neq e$ and $r\in {\mathbb N}$, is open and
dense in ${\rm Aut}(X, \nu)$. Their intersection is comeager. If $S$ belongs to this intersection,
then $d_{\mathrm u}(v^{T,S},\mathrm{id})=1$ for every $v\neq e$.              
                                                         
Hence $\alpha^{T,S}$ is essentially
free.

label: prop:F2-prime-twm
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:F2-prime-twm}
Let $T\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ be a mixing and prime transformation. There exists a pointwise weakly mixing p.m.p.\ action
$\rho$ of ${\mathbb F}_2=\langle a,b\rangle$ on $(X,\nu)$
with $\rho(a)=T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $T$ is mixing, it is
aperiodic, so
Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:generic-second-generator}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   gives
$S\in{\rm Aut}(X,\nu)$ such that $\alpha := \alpha^{T,S}$ is an essentially free p.m.p.\ action of ${\mathbb F}_2$ on $(X,\nu)$. This
action is ergodic because its restriction to $\langle a\rangle$ is mixing.

                                                                         
                                
                                             
                                                         
Note that the proof of
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{wrobel2026orbit} begins by replacing the given essentially free
ergodic action by an orbit equivalent one whose first generator is mixing;
it is only this replacement that we must avoid, since we insist on the
prescribed $T$, and everything after it applies verbatim to $\alpha$. This
is the sole reason why
Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:generic-second-generator}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   was needed.

Let $[T]$ be the full group of the orbit equivalence relation generated by
$T$, a Polish group in the uniform metric
\cite[Proposition~3.2]{kechris2010global} and hence a Baire space. For
$\phi\in[T]$, set
$ \beta_\phi = \alpha^{T, S \phi}$.
                                               
By \cite[Lemma~2.2]{wrobel2026orbit}, every $\beta_\phi$ is essentially free
and generates the same orbit equivalence relation as $\alpha$.

For $w\in{\mathbb F}_2\setminus\{e\}$, let $Z_w$ be the set of
$\phi\in[T]$ for which $\beta_\phi(w)$ is weakly mixing.
We claim that $Z_w$ is comeager in $[T]$. Write $w=uvu^{-1}$ with $v$ cyclically reduced.     
                                                                     
                                                                         
By passing to a conjugate automorphism we may assume that $w=v$. If $v=a^{k}$ with $k\neq0$, then
$\beta_\phi(v)=T^{k}$ is mixing for every $\phi$. Otherwise $b^{\pm1}$
occurs in $v$, and \cite[Lemmas~3.1 and~3.2]{wrobel2026orbit} together with
the Baire category theorem show that the set ${\mathcal E}_v^{C_v}\subseteq[T]$ of
\cite[Section~3]{wrobel2026orbit} is comeager; by
\cite[Proposition~2.1]{wrobel2026orbit}, $\beta_\phi(v)$ is weakly mixing
for every $\phi\in{\mathcal E}_v^{C_v}$. This proves the claim.

Intersecting comeager sets $Z_w$ over
the countable set ${\mathbb F}_2\setminus\{e\}$, we obtain $\phi$ for which the action $\rho=\beta_\phi$ is pointwise weakly mixing.

Finally, every $\rho$-invariant factor is invariant under
$\rho(a)=T$. Since $T$ is prime, such a factor is trivial or the whole
system. Hence $\rho$ is prime. This finishes the proof.

label: thm:all-free-ranks
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:all-free-ranks}
For every $2\leq n\leq\infty$, there exists an essentially free, prime, pointwise weakly
mixing p.m.p.\ action of ${\mathbb F}_n$. These actions may be chosen as restrictions
of one action of ${\mathbb F}_2$ to the nested free subgroups
$H_2\leq H_3\leq\cdots\leq H_\infty$ defined above.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Identify ${\mathbb F}_n$ with $H_n$ and restrict the action $\rho$ from
Proposition~ 
    \IfBooleanTF{prop:F2-prime-twm}{\paper@unboxedref*{#2}}{ 
      \begingroup
      \edef\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}{\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}} 
      \expandafter\paper@styledref\getrefbykeydefault{#2}{anchor}{}.\@nil{#2} 
      \endgroup
    } 
   to $H_n$.                               
                                                                           
                                                           
If
$\mathcal A$ is an $H_n$-invariant factor, then it is invariant under
$a\in H_n$, hence under the prime transformation $\rho(a)=T$. Therefore
$\mathcal A$ is trivial or the whole system and  the restricted action is prime.
The rest is an easy check.
